extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Plato and political/philosophical theory
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and extraction of normative principles from Plato's Republic (Book IV–V material): virtues of the ideal State, structure of the soul, educational and social rules for guardians, and related political prescriptions. Useful for scholars, students, or writers summarizing Platonic political theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of duty over happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary aim in founding the State is the well‑being of the State, not the happiness of individual citizens; guardians are to be guardians, not holiday‑makers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that making citizens happy is not the principal aim; duty precedes happiness. The passage argues that the greatest individual happiness may differ from ordinary notions of happiness and that moral law (right) has firmer claim than utilitarian calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility as a corrective but not the foundation of ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: The utilitarian principle is valuable as a corrective and is often coextensive with right, but it is not the historical or true foundation of morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges utility's usefulness in many human actions, but distinguishes it from the primary moral principles ('truth' and 'right'), noting happiness's ambiguities and limited appeal to higher nature. Use utility for application where fitting, but not as first principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity of 'happiness' as evaluative standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The term ‘happiness’ has several senses—pleasure vs. ideal life, subjective vs. objective, temporal vs. otherworldly, self‑regarding vs. universal—which complicates using it as a clear standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns against equating happiness with mere comforts; in major trials or heroic acts happiness is scarcely thought of. Evaluations should specify which sense of happiness is meant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political expediency must be governed by right and truth
rubrics_metrics.description: In politics, expediency (usefulness) must be interpreted as the law of right limited by social conditions; right and truth are the highest aims of government and should not be abandoned for temporal interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy should appeal to the better mind of nations and leaders must often act above ambition; practical measures are judged by their conformity with higher ideals, not merely by short‑term utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whole (unity/harmony) as foundational principle in politics and art
rubrics_metrics.description: The conception of the whole lies at the foundation of both politics and art; criticism and political order rest on harmony, symmetry, measure, proportion, and unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative judgments should privilege unity and harmonious proportion—the state or artwork is assessed by how its parts form a coherent, ordered whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on State size (modelled on Greek cities)
rubrics_metrics.description: The State should be limited in size, following the traditional Greek model where small city‑states were ideal; size has moral and political consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is invoked to justify limits on expansion and to ground other institutional designs (division of labour, social cohesion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labour as justice (every one doing his own business)
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice in the State is primarily the principle that each person performs the role suited to his nature—‘every one having his own’—and injustice arises when people do another’s business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of social organization should check for clear role‑allocation and avoidance of dangerous role‑mixing (e.g., a cobbler becoming a guardian).

rubrics_metrics.name: Four cardinal virtues as criteria for the State and individual
rubrics_metrics.description: The State and individual will contain four virtues—wisdom, courage, temperance, and justice—and their presence defines political virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each virtue corresponds to a class in the State and a part of the soul; full political/moral evaluation examines all four and their interrelations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wisdom (politic skill of the guardians)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wisdom is the skill of those who advise on the interests of the whole State (the guardians): a concentrated political wisdom in a small ruling class makes the State wise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess rulers by their practical, deliberative skill in serving the common good, distinct from technical crafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage defined as preservation of right opinion about dangers
rubrics_metrics.description: Courage is the preservation of the opinions which law and education have prescribed concerning dangers; education (ground) and laws (colour) fix these opinions so they resist pleasure and pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of courage should emphasize stable, law‑rooted responses to danger rather than mere animal bravado; education and legal inculcation are central to producing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance as harmony/mastery of better principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperance is the harmony in which the better principle masters the worse; in the State it is a diffused harmony that unites upper, middle, and lower classes in one mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temperance is assessed by the degree of internal harmony and mutual self‑control across classes and parts of the soul; it resembles musical harmony rather than a single faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as universal order (each part doing its own work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is the perfect order by which all natures and classes do their own business—the right man in the right place—making the State and soul healthy and well‑ordered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice is evaluated as systemic order and cooperation; morally good actions form good habits and justice is akin to the health of the soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdependence and hierarchy of virtues (justice as foundation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is more abstract and foundational than the other virtues and is the universal idea to which the others are referred; the virtues may be distinguished by degree rather than kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging moral systems, consider whether justice (order) grounds other virtues and whether the proposed definitions capture this foundational role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence between State classes and soul parts
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a one‑to‑one correspondence: guardians/rulers ≈ reason, soldiers ≈ spirit/passion, producers ≈ appetite/desire; virtues in the State mirror virtues in individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this mapping to evaluate institutional designs and moral psychology—each social class should embody the corresponding soul part's virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological criterion for distinct faculties: contradictory functioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Different faculties are distinguished by their capacity to produce opposite effects in the same relation; if two impulses are contradictory, they arise from distinct principles in the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this test when analyzing mental structure: look for contradictory motivates (e.g., thirst vs. rational restraint) to infer multiple faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of education (music and gymnastics) in harmonizing soul and society
rubrics_metrics.description: Education (music and gymnastics) and laws lay the ground and dye the colours of opinion so that desirable dispositions (courage, temperance) become fixed and resistant to pleasure/pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate educational systems by their ability to inculcate stable right opinions and harmonize the soul's parts; formative institutions are decisive for virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic inclusion by aptitude not sex
rubrics_metrics.description: If women are of the same kind as men in aptitude (though possibly in a lesser degree), they should receive the same education and share the same employments (music, gymnastics, war).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess role allocation by actual capacities rather than nominal sex differences; choose the best (regardless of sex) for guardianship and training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of controlled mating and population policy for civic excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: The rulers must manage marriages and breeding (hymeneal festivals, pairing the good with the good, eliminating inferior offspring) to preserve the city’s quality; nobles may use deliberate falsehoods to accomplish this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are prescriptive institutional mechanisms in Plato’s design: evaluate them as part of a eugenic/social engineering scheme aimed at producing guardian excellence, noting moral and practical implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age and legal rules for parenthood and marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: Specified prime childbearing ages are mandated (men ~25–55; women ~20–40); marriages outside prescribed ages or without rulers’ consent are impious; degrees of affinity are regulated even under communal arrangements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These precise demographic/legal rules are part of the guardians' regime; assess feasibility and ethical consequences when considering similar policy proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common property and communal households to secure unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Common property, communal houses, and shared meals among guardians are designed to eliminate private interests and ensure unity; in such a polity private pleasures and pecuniary disputes vanish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate social cohesion by testing for private property conflicts; communal arrangements are judged by their effect on unity and preventing strife, and by their impact on individual happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training of young guardians through exposure and mentorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Young warriors and guardians must be trained by exposure (observing battles, crafts) and under experienced veterans; practical training (e.g., teaching a youth to ride) is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess military and vocational education by apprenticeship, supervised exposure to practice, and graduated responsibility—avoid reckless exposure to danger while permitting controlled risk for skill.
